summary: This unit teaches you to provide food and beverage service in a villa dining area: prepare the dining room and the service station, lay a standard cover, understand menus and styles of service, greet and seat guests, take orders accurately, serve and clear food and drinks safely, serve alcohol responsibly, look after guests with special needs, handle complaints, prepare bills and take payment, and close down the dining area. You will work hygienically and safely throughout.

blocks.p: Meals are often the high point of a stay in a villa. A well-set table, a polite greeting, a correct order and a hot plate served quietly make guests feel looked after. A fork on the floor, a wrong order or a cold dish does the opposite. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. It covers table service for a small group of guests, where one team often does everything from setting the table to closing down.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and a group practical where you set a dinner table, serve a three-course dinner to four guests, and run a breakfast buffet with beverage service and a complaint. The assessor watches your grooming, hygiene, covers, order taking, serving, clearing and teamwork.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Hygiene, grooming and safety in the dining area

ul: Clean, pressed uniform; clean shoes.
Hair neat and tied back or covered; **short, clean nails** (no long painted nails).
**Wash your hands** before work, after the toilet, after touching your face or hair, after handling money, after clearing and before handling clean cutlery or food.
Light or no perfume, because strong smells affect guests' enjoyment of food. No jingling bracelets.
If you have a cut, cover it with a clean waterproof plaster; if you are ill (vomiting, diarrhoea, fever), tell your supervisor and do not handle food or drink.

blocks.h: Why you do not touch your face or hair

blocks.p: Germs pass from your hands to food, cutlery and glasses. Touching your face or hair while serving is a hygiene risk for every guest, not a matter of make-up or hairstyle.

head: Item
Hold it by
Why
rows: Cutlery
The handle
No fingermarks or germs where guests eat
Glasses
The stem or base, never the rim or inside
Clean rim, no fingermarks, no germs
Plates
The rim, with the thumb off the food
Food stays clean
Cups
The body or handle, never the rim
Keeps the rim clean

blocks.p: **Check cutlery and glasses** by holding each to the light. They must be clean, dry and not chipped or cracked. Take any damaged item out of use. If a guest drops a fork, bring a clean fork first, then pick up the dropped one and take it away.

head: Hazard
What you do
rows: Spilled drink on a tiled floor
Put out a wet-floor sign and wipe it up at once
Heavy loaded tray
Carry it close to the body, heaviest items in the centre, supported on the palm
Hot plates and dishes
Use a service cloth and warn the guest: 'Caution, hot plate'
Broken glass
Stop; sweep up and dispose of it safely (never pick it up with bare hands); check around
Cables and trolleys
Keep walkways clear; push trolleys, do not pull
Lifting tables and chairs
Ask for help; lift together

blocks.note: Keep hot food at about 63 °C or above and cold food at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says. Use a serving tool for each dish so allergens are not passed from one dish to another.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: A Food Handler's Permit from the local health department is required for anyone who serves food or drink in Jamaica. Check yours is valid.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Preparing the dining area and the service station

flow: Attend the briefing: menu, specials, numbers, allergies, VIPs
Clean and check the dining area
Check your own grooming and walk the area

ul: **The briefing** shares the menu, the specials and any guest allergies. It is not for deciding who goes home early, sharing tips or planning days off.
Check the booking: number of guests, time, special requests, birthdays or anniversaries.
Clean the floor, tables, chairs and windows. Check lights, fans and music.
Chairs steady and clean; table not wobbling (fold a coaster under a short leg).
Use a clean, ironed cloth with the centre fold running down the middle of the table.
Make sure the drop is the same on all sides and does not touch the floor.
Lay it without shaking it in the guests' area.

blocks.p: A **cover** is the cutlery, glass and napkin for one guest. A standard cover for a three-course dinner of soup, main course and dessert is:

head: Item
Where it goes
rows: Show plate or main plate (if used)
In the centre, 2 cm from the table edge
Main knife
On the **right**, cutting edge turned **in** (towards the plate)
Soup spoon
On the right, outside the knife (used first)
Main fork
On the **left** of the plate
Side (bread) plate and butter knife
On the **left**, outside the fork
Dessert spoon and fork
**Above** the plate, handles pointing right (spoon) and left (fork)
Water glass
**Above the tip of the main knife**
Wine glasses (if used)
In a line to the right of the water glass
Napkin
In the centre of the plate, or on the left of the forks, folded neatly

blocks.p: Cutlery is placed in order of use, from the outside in. Set the cover so that everything is about 1 to 2 cm from the edge of the table and in a straight line.

ul: Stand at the guest's seat: is the cover straight, clean and complete?
Hold cutlery and glasses to the light, check the napkin is clean.
Salt, pepper, a small arrangement of flowers or a candle in the centre and a menu if used.

blocks.p: The service station is a side table or cupboard holding the extra items you need during service, so you do not leave the dining area.

ul: Spare cutlery, napkins, glasses, side plates
Trays, service cloths, order pads (dockets), pens
Menus, water jugs, ice and condiments
Tongs and serving spoons
A cloth and a small brush for crumbing down

blocks.p: Before your shift ends, **restock the station** so that the next shift has what it needs to start service.

head: Menu
What it is
rows: À la carte
Each dish is priced and ordered on its own
Table d'hôte
A set menu of a fixed number of courses at one fixed price
Breakfast menu
Often a buffet or set breakfast, such as ackee and saltfish, callaloo, fried dumplings, fruit, eggs, Jamaican chocolate tea
Special
A dish offered for one day only; servers tell guests about it
Drinks list
The wines, beers, soft drinks, juices and cocktails available

head: Style
How it works
Server's main job
rows: Plated service
The kitchen puts the food on each plate
Carry plates safely and serve each guest by seat number
Silver service
The server serves food from a dish onto the guest's plate with a spoon and fork (service spoon and fork), from the guest's left
Skilled use of service spoon and fork; hot dishes; speed and neatness
Buffet
Guests help themselves from a display of dishes
Keep dishes full, tidy, labelled and at the right temperature; give each dish its own tool
Family-style
Dishes put on the table and shared
Refill dishes, clear when finished
Counter or drinks service
Order and collect at the bar
Serve quickly and politely

blocks.note: In buffet service the server does not carry plates from the kitchen to the table, cook to order in front of guests or take payment at the door. The server keeps the dishes full, tidy and at the right temperature, and watches for guests who need help.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Label each dish with its name and allergy notes (nuts, milk, egg, gluten, shellfish).
Give every dish a **serving tool**, and replace it if it falls.
Keep hot food hot (chafing dishes) and cold food cold (on ice).
Refill before a dish runs out; do not top up a half-empty dish with old food.
Wipe spills, remove empty trays and keep the area tidy.

flow: Greet guests with a smile at the entrance
Show them to their table, pull out chairs if needed

ul: Do not hand them the bill, make them wait outside or leave them alone for half an hour.
Offer a high chair for small children, and seat guests who use a wheelchair where they have room.
Ask whether anyone has an **allergy** or dislikes.

blocks.p: Take the order standing at the guest's left (or as your Centre says) with your pad (docket) in your hand.

ol: Give each guest a **seat number**. Seat 1 is the guest by the entrance or the host, and the numbers go clockwise.
Write the dish beside the seat number: '2 – jerk chicken, well done, no onion'.
Ask about cooking, sides and any change (for example how a steak should be cooked).
Check allergies and tell the kitchen.
**Repeat the order back** to the guests to be sure you have it right before it goes to the kitchen.
Give the docket (order) to the kitchen and keep a copy at the station.

blocks.p: Seat numbers mean each guest gets the right dish without being asked 'Who has the fish?'.

ul: Mention a drink or side dish that goes well with the dish: 'The rice and peas go very well with the jerk chicken.'
Do not insist, keep asking or add things to the order without telling the guest.

blocks.p: A guest asks, 'Is there any nut in the rum cake?' If you are not sure, **do not guess**. Check with the cook and then tell the guest what you find out. Never tell the guest to 'try a little'.

blocks.h: When the kitchen cannot make a dish

blocks.p: Apologise, explain politely and suggest the closest dish. Never promise something that will not come.

ul: Carry plates by the rim, thumb off the food.
Carry only as many as you can hold safely. Never stack plates on top of each other or carry more than your skill allows.
Use a tray for several plates or for glasses.
Warn guests of hot plates.
Serve by **seat number**, working clockwise, without reaching across guests.
Guests of honour or older guests are often served first, and the **host last**. Children are served early. House rules may differ.
Serve food from the guest's **left**, and clear from the guest's **right**, unless house rules say otherwise.
Place the main item (meat or fish) **nearest the guest**, with vegetables and starch behind or beside.

flow: Check the docket and the seat number
Collect the plate and check it
Say the dish name and warn about heat
Step back and check the guest needs nothing more

blocks.note: When guests are in a private conversation, wait for a pause, say 'Excuse me' and serve quietly. Do not speak loudly over them, leave plates on a side table or join the talk.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Between courses: crumbing down and clearing

ul: Clear the plates **when all the guests at the table have finished**. A guest who has finished usually puts the knife and fork **together on the plate**.
Clear quietly from the guest's right, without stacking at the table, and take the plates away.
Before dessert remove salt and pepper, side plates and used glasses not needed, and **brush crumbs** from the cloth with a cloth and small brush or folded napkin (crumbing down).
Do not remove water glasses, napkins or the dessert cutlery already set.
Never clear one guest's plate while others are still eating; do not clear half-finished plates to 'save time'.
Use tongs for bread rolls, not your hands.
Do not put your fingers on food or inside glasses.
Do not wipe cutlery on your own cloth and reuse it.
Keep a clean service cloth for hot plates and another to wipe spills.

head: Fault
Better practice
rows: Reaching across a guest
Move round, or ask the guest to pass
Stacking dirty plates in front of guests
Clear one by one onto the tray or at the service station
Serving the plate with the sauce nearest the guest
Main item nearest the guest
Using the same serving spoon for two dishes
One tool for each dish

ul: Offer water as soon as guests are seated. Serve a sealed bottle by opening it at the table and pouring in front of the guest.
Serve cold drinks in a tall highball glass with ice, **ice first, then the drink**.
Always use an ice scoop, never a glass or your hands.
Serve drinks from the guest's **right**, hold the glass by the base or stem, and place it above the knife tip.
Carry glasses upright on a tray, held level, never by the rims or stacked.

head: Glass
Used for
rows: Highball
Tall juices, soft drinks, mixed drinks with ice
Wine glass (bowl, stem, foot)
Red and white wine
Flute
Sparkling wine for a toast
Tumbler
Water, short drinks, rum on ice
Cup and saucer
Tea and coffee; the handle points to the guest's right

head: Drink
What it is
rows: Sorrel
A drink made from the dried red sepals of the sorrel (hibiscus) plant, with ginger, often served at Christmas
Ginger beer
A fizzy or fresh drink flavoured with ginger
Chocolate tea
A hot breakfast drink made from grated local cocoa
Blue Mountain coffee
Jamaica's best-known coffee
Fruit punch, June plum, cane juice
Fresh juices and mixed drinks

flow: Show the bottle to the host, label facing him
Open it at the table: cut the foil, draw the cork or open the cap, wipe the neck
Pour a small amount for the host to taste
Serve the guests, ladies first and the host last (or as house rules say)
Place the bottle on the table or in a cooler

ul: Pour a glass only **a third to a half** full. Do not fill it to the brim.
Dry white and sparkling wines are usually served well chilled. Red wines are served cool, at room temperature.
Hold the bottle low on the label side; do not touch the glass with it; turn the bottle slightly to avoid a drip.
The legal age to be sold alcohol in Jamaica is **18**. If a guest looks young, **politely ask for photo ID**.
Do not serve a guest who is drunk. Kindly refuse, offer water or a soft drink and tell your supervisor.
Do not serve a double to save a trip; do not ask someone else to buy for them; do not let a guest pour his own drinks behind the bar.

head: Signs a guest has had too much
Your action
rows: Slurred speech, unsteady, loud, spilling drinks
Stop serving alcohol, politely
Aggressive or upset
Stay calm, get the supervisor
Cannot get home safely
Help arrange safe transport

blocks.note: Serving alcohol is a legal responsibility. The villa needs a spirit licence, and serving drunk guests or under-age people can put the licence and the guests at risk.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Guests with special needs, and complaints

head: Guest
What to do
rows: A guest with a food allergy
Ask what the allergy is; check with the cook; use clean tools and a clean plate; mark the order; keep the dish apart; tell the guest what you found and double-check before serving
A family with a small child
Offer a high chair and a child's portion; place hot dishes and sharp knives out of reach; serve the child early
A guest who uses a wheelchair
Ask where the guest would like to sit; remove a chair to make space; speak to the guest, not the companion
A vegetarian or vegan guest
Check what the dish contains (stock, cheese, egg); suggest suitable dishes
A guest who speaks little English
Speak slowly, point to the menu, repeat the order

flow: Put it right (for example a fresh hot dish)

head: Complaint
Best response
rows: Cold fish
Apologise, take the plate and ask the kitchen for a hot one
A dish has run out
Apologise and suggest the closest dish
Coffee is cold
Apologise, take the cup and bring a fresh hot one

ul: Do not say that fish is often served cool, that the cook is busy, or leave the plate and quietly take it off the bill.
Tell the supervisor even when you have solved it, so the complaint is **recorded** and the cause can be stopped. It is not to blame someone, to charge the guest or to hide it from the owner.
A complaint **form** records the complaint and the action.
Check that every item ordered is on the bill, that the prices are right and the total is right. Do not check whether a tip has been added in for you.

Taxes such as GCT (General Consumption Tax) and any service charge are added as the current rules and the villa's policy say. Do not guess a rate; use the figure on the bill system or ask your supervisor.
Present the bill in a **clean folder**, placed face down near the guest who asked for it, not read aloud or handed to the youngest guest.

head: Payment
What you do
rows: Cash in J$
Count it in front of the guest; give change and a receipt
Card
Take the card to the machine politely, or bring the machine to the table; never take the card out of sight; return the card and receipt
US$
Use the exchange rate set by the manager for that day

head: Question
Working
Answer
rows: A guest pays a J$6,350 bill with a J$10,000 note. Change?
The manager's rate that day is J$150 to US$1. A bill of J$9,000 is paid in US$. How much?
US$60

blocks.p: Work every sum twice. The rate above is made up for the example. Your manager sets the rate each day.

flow: Clear all tables and take everything to the wash-up
Wipe tables, sweep and mop the floor, put out a wet floor sign
Clean and store condiments and equipment as the house rules say
Put dirty linen in the linen bag or hamper, away from food
Report faults and low stock to the supervisor

ul: Wipe the sauce and other condiment bottles and store them as house rules say. Do not leave them out on the tables overnight, pour them together or throw away nearly full ones.
Dirty table linen goes into a linen bag, away from food; never into the bin or shaken out on the terrace.
Restock so the next shift can start.
Report equipment faults and items running low.

blocks.p: Tick each statement when you can do it without looking at your notes.

ul: I can groom myself and wash my hands at the right times.
I can hold cutlery, glasses and plates correctly and check them for cleanliness and damage.
I can prepare the dining area and stock the service station.
I can lay a standard cover and say where each item goes.
I can say the differences between à la carte, table d'hôte, buffet, plated and silver service.
I can greet and seat guests and offer water and menus.
I can take an order with seat numbers, check allergies and repeat it back.
I can carry plates and trays safely and serve by seat number.
I can clear when all guests have finished and crumb down before dessert.
I can serve drinks from the right, pour wine correctly and serve alcohol responsibly.
I can look after guests with allergies, children or a wheelchair.
I can handle a complaint and report it.
I can present a bill, take payment and give correct change.
I can close down and restock.

terms: Cover
The cutlery, glass and napkin for one guest
Mise en place
Having everything in place before service
À la carte
Each dish priced and ordered on its own
Table d'hôte
A set menu at one fixed price
Silver service
Serving food from a dish onto the guest's plate with a spoon and fork
Buffet
Guests help themselves from a display of dishes
Docket
The written order sent to the kitchen
Seat number
A number given to each guest so dishes go to the right person
Service station
The side table holding extra items for service
Crumbing down
Brushing crumbs off the cloth before dessert
Cloche
A dome that covers a plate to keep food hot
Service cloth
A cloth carried to hold hot plates and wipe drips
GCT
General Consumption Tax, added to most bills
Sorrel
A Jamaican drink made from hibiscus sepals
Responsible service of alcohol
Checking age and refusing guests who are drunk
Food Handler's Permit
Permit required for food and drink handlers

c1.title: A breakfast buffet at a villa in Ocho Rios
c1.text: Six guests are staying at a villa in Ocho Rios, and you are setting up the breakfast buffet at 7:00 a.m. The dishes are ackee and saltfish, scrambled eggs, fried dumplings, fresh fruit, and a bowl of porridge made with coconut milk. One guest, Mr. Hall, has told you he is allergic to shellfish and another is allergic to wheat. You have one serving spoon and two dishes that need one.

c2.title: A birthday dinner in Negril
c2.text: A group of six guests is booked for dinner at 7:30 p.m. at a villa in Negril, to celebrate Miss Andrea's birthday. The menu is soup, jerk chicken or grilled snapper, and rum cake. Trainee Rohan is setting the table. He has laid the cloth and now sets the first cover. A second trainee, Kimberly, will serve. The host, Mr. Edwards, sits at the head of the table.

c3.title: Wine and a young guest in Montego Bay
c3.text: At a villa in Montego Bay, the guests choose a bottle of white wine. The host, Mr. Cole, is celebrating with his wife and their friend Marcia, who looks about 17. Server Dwayne brings the bottle. Later, another guest at the next table, Mr. Tulloch, has been drinking all evening, is loud and asks Dwayne for another large rum.

c4.title: A wrong dish at a villa in Mandeville
c4.text: At a villa in Mandeville, Mrs. Blake ordered the grilled snapper. When Shanice serves it, she finds that Mrs. Blake has been given jerk chicken instead, and she is hungry because the table is already finished with its soup. The restaurant is full and Shanice is carrying three plates.

c5.title: The bill and payment in Port Antonio
c5.text: Four guests finish dinner at a villa in Port Antonio. The bill, including everything, is J$12,600. The host, Mr. Pinnock, pays with a J$20,000 note. Later, an American guest at another table wants to pay a bill of J$13,500 in US dollars. The manager has set the rate for the day at J$150 for US$1.

c6.title: Closing down at the end of the night
c6.text: After dinner service at a villa in Treasure Beach, Marlon is closing down. A guest has spilled a drink near the terrace door, there is a broken wine glass on the floor of the service station and dirty table napkins are lying on the counter beside the clean plates. The condiment bottles are still on the tables.

questions.q: What should you put out at the buffet for each dish?
o: One serving spoon shared between all of the dishes
A label with allergy notes and its own serving tool
A sign showing the price of each dish on offer
A list of the guests who may eat each dish
questions.why: Each dish needs a label and its own tool so allergens are not carried from one dish to another. Sharing a spoon spreads allergens.

questions.q: Mr. Hall is allergic to shellfish. What should you do?
o: Tell him to avoid the saltfish and trust that the rest is safe
Serve him from every dish and watch to see if he reacts
Tell him it is safe as long as he eats only a small amount
Check with the cook which dishes have shellfish and tell the team
questions.why: Allergies can be dangerous, so you check with the cook and tell the guest and the team what you find out. Never guess or let him test a dish.

questions.q: At 7:45 a.m. the ackee dish is half empty. What should you do?
o: Refill it with fresh, hot food before it runs out
Wait until it is empty and then fill it
Top it up with the leftovers from yesterday
Remove the dish and say it is finished
questions.why: Refill before a dish runs out so guests never face an empty dish. Never mix in old food. Keep it at the right temperature.

questions.q: What temperature should the hot dishes be kept at, or as the Centre's food safety plan says?
o: About 40 °C
About 20 °C
About 63 °C or above
About 5 °C
questions.why: Hot food is kept at about 63 °C or above to prevent bacteria growing. Cold food is kept at 5 °C or below.

questions.q: Where does Rohan place the main knife?
o: On the left of the plate, with the edge turned out
Above the plate, with the handle pointing left
On the right of the plate, with the cutting edge turned in
On the right of the plate, with the cutting edge turned out
questions.why: The main knife goes on the right with its cutting edge turned towards the plate. The fork goes on the left.

questions.q: Where does Rohan place the water glass?
o: Above the tip of the main knife
On the left, next to the side plate
In the centre of the plate
Above the forks
questions.why: The water glass goes above the tip of the main knife, with wine glasses in a line beside it.

questions.q: In which order should Kimberly serve the main course?
o: Starting with the host, then the guests in clockwise order
Starting with the youngest guest, then whoever is nearest
Whichever plates the kitchen puts out first, to save time
By seat number, the guest of honour early and the host last
questions.why: Plates are served by seat number, usually with the guest of honour early and the host last, to avoid reaching across anyone. House rules may vary.

questions.q: Miss Andrea asks whether the jerk chicken has nuts. Kimberly does not know. What should she do?
o: Say there are no nuts because jerk seasoning has none
Check with the cook and tell the guest what she finds
Tell Miss Andrea to taste a small piece
Suggest the snapper without checking anything
questions.why: Never guess about an allergy. Check with the cook and report the answer to the guest.

questions.q: How should Dwayne present the white wine?
o: Open it in the kitchen and pour it for everyone
Show the label to the host, open it at the table and pour a little for him to taste
Pour a full glass for the first guest
Open it at the table and serve the host first, filling his glass to the brim
questions.why: The host checks the label and tastes the wine before it is served. Only a third to a half of a glass is poured.

questions.q: Marcia looks about 17 and wants a glass of the wine. What should Dwayne do?
o: Serve her a small glass, since the host is paying for it
Ask Mr. Cole whether it is all right and serve if he agrees
Politely ask for photo ID, and offer a soft drink if she has none
Serve her half a glass and watch that she does not finish it
questions.why: Under-age guests must not be sold alcohol, even if a parent is present. Ask for ID and offer another drink.

questions.q: What should Dwayne do when Mr. Tulloch asks for another large rum?
o: Politely refuse, offer water or a soft drink, tell the supervisor
Serve a smaller rum than usual to calm him down a little
Serve the rum, because he is paying and the night is busy
Let him pour his own drink from the bottle at the table
questions.why: A guest who is drunk must not be served more. Offer an alternative and tell the supervisor.

questions.q: What should Shanice do first about the wrong dish?
o: Tell Mrs. Blake that the chicken is just as good as the fish
Ask Mrs. Blake to eat the chicken, and take the fish off the bill
Say that the kitchen made the mistake and walk away
Apologise, take the plate and check the docket for the right order
questions.why: The guest has the right dish ordered, so the first step is to apologise, take the plate and check the docket. Excuses, or asking her to accept it, do not solve the problem.

questions.q: What would best have prevented the mix-up?
o: Asking guests to carry their own dishes from the kitchen
Taking orders only from the host of each table
Serving every table the same dish of the day
Writing seat numbers on the docket and reading the order back
questions.why: Seat numbers and a read-back make sure each dish matches the right guest and that the kitchen has the right order.

questions.q: How should Shanice carry the three plates?
o: Stacked on top of each other so that she can carry more
By the rim, thumbs off the food, a tray for the rest
Held out at arm's length so nothing spills on her uniform
By the food side, so that the rims stay clean for guests
questions.why: Plates are carried by the rim with the thumb away from the food, only as many as can be held safely. Stacking or holding by the food is unsafe.

questions.q: How much change does Mr. Pinnock receive?
questions.why: 20,000 − 12,600 = 7,400. The other answers come from arithmetic slips.

questions.q: How much must the American guest pay in US$?
o: US$90
US$85
questions.why: 13,500 ÷ 150 = 90, so the bill is US$90. Dividing by the wrong rate or multiplying gives the other figures.

questions.q: How should the bill be presented to Mr. Pinnock?
o: In a clean folder, face down, near him
Read aloud across the room
Handed to the youngest guest
Left on the table with the main course
questions.why: A folder, face down, near the host is private and polite. Reading it aloud or leaving it early is not.

questions.q: What should Marlon do about the spilled drink near the terrace door?
o: Leave it to dry in the warm air
Cover it with a napkin until the morning
Tell guests to walk around it
Put out a wet floor sign and wipe it up at once
questions.why: Spills are slip hazards and must be wiped at once, with a sign until the floor is dry.

questions.q: What should Marlon do about the broken glass in the service station?
o: Pick the pieces up with bare hands and drop them in the bin
Sweep it up carefully, dispose of it safely and check around
Leave it where it is until the cleaner arrives tomorrow
Push it into a corner under the counter, out of sight
questions.why: Broken glass is swept up and disposed of carefully so nobody is cut. Never use bare hands.

questions.q: Where should the dirty table napkins go, and why?
o: Beside the clean plates, ready for the morning wash
In the bin, since new ones cost less than washing
In a linen bag or hamper, kept away from the food
Shaken out on the terrace and folded to use again
questions.why: Dirty linen goes into a bag or hamper away from food and clean items to prevent contamination.
